name: Symmetry and Beauty in City Photos (rating + keep/delete)
description:
Faithful replication of Study 1 (urban photography) of Gartus, Valuch, Hakala, Peltoketo, Pelowski & Leder, "Symmetry Suits Cities, but Not Nature or Food: Image Beauty Effects Across Urban, Nature, and Food Photography" (manuscript submitted for publication; data and stimuli on OSF tvqeg, DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/TVQEG, CC BY 4.0). The 160 stimuli are the authors' own Study 1 images from that OSF project, used with credit to the authors.

What participants do: after demographics (age, gender, country, education, student, full-time work), each participant is randomly given one of the two original stimulus sets: 80 city photos, 40 cropped symmetrically around the scene's axis (CenterCrop) and 40 shifted crops (ShiftedLeft / ShiftedRight); each of the 80 scenes appears in only one version per set. They do two tasks on the same 80 photos, in random order of tasks (counterbalanced, as in the original): (1) rate how beautiful each photo is, 1 = not beautiful to 7 = very beautiful; (2) decide for each photo whether to keep or delete it, as if it were in their own photo collection (buttons, swipe or arrow keys). Response times are recorded from image onset. A post-task questionnaire follows: familiarity with the places (1–7) and an open question on its influence, an open question on what drove keep decisions and high ratings, how much 15 factors were considered when judging beauty (1–7), importance of image beauty and of the depicted object's beauty for keeping photos of 7 genres, photo-taking frequency for 7 genres, amateur / professional photography, and camera equipment.

What the original found: the manuscript's title gives the result, symmetry raises the beauty of urban photos but not of nature or food photos. In the open Study 1 data (80 participants), symmetric crops got a mean beauty rating of 4.09 vs 3.96 for shifted crops and were kept 57.0% vs 53.4% of the time.

Data: design = { stimulus_set, task_order }; beauty = { beauty } per image, rating_rt = { rt_ms }, swipe = { choice: keep | delete, rt_ms }, all keyed by the image file name without .jpg (same as trial_img on OSF). Symmetry condition and source scene can be read from the key. Analysis as in the original: mixed models with participant and source image as random effects, comparing symmetric vs nonsymmetric versions for rating and keep probability.

Differences from the original study: (1) the 25-item Visual Aesthetic Sensitivity Test (VAST) used in the original is left out because its items are a copyrighted test; (2) task instructions and the swipe screen are written for this template (the OSF files give the variables, not the exact instructions); (3) the anchors of the beauty-importance and object-importance scales (1 = not important at all, 7 = very important) and the factor labels of the appreciation matrix are written out from the variable names; (4) images are recompressed JPEGs at the original 1200 × 900 px; (5) open answers for 'other' country / education and field of study / profession are not asked; (6) English wording; the original sample was mostly from Austria and Germany. Only Study 1 (urban) is rebuilt; Studies 2–4 (nature, food, mixed genres) use other image sets on the same OSF project.
author: Gartus, Valuch, Hakala, Peltoketo, Pelowski & Leder

elements.name: consent

elements.title: Are you currently a university student?

elements.name: design
elements.title: Assigned condition
elements.description: { stimulus_set: 'set_1' | 'set_2', task_order: 'ratingfirst' | 'swipingfirst' }, drawn at random per participant, as in the original data.

elements.name: beauty
elements.title: How beautiful do you find this image?
elements.description: Rating task: 80 images in random order, 1 = not beautiful … 7 = very beautiful; the next image appears on click. key = image file name without .jpg (same as trial_img on OSF tvqeg). Symmetry condition = CenterCrop (symmetric) vs ShiftedLeft/ShiftedRight (nonsymmetric) in the key; the source scene = the part before the first _Center/_Shifted.

elements.name: rating_rt
elements.title: Rating response time
elements.description: { rt_ms } per image, from image onset to the click on the rating button; same keys as beauty.

elements.name: swipe
elements.title: Keep or delete this image?
elements.description: Swiping task on the same 80 images in a new random order: { choice: 'keep' | 'delete', rt_ms } per image (rt from image onset). Same keys as beauty. The original analysis compares the share of 'keep' and the beauty ratings between symmetric and nonsymmetric versions (mixed models with participant and source image as random effects).

elements.name: familiarity
elements.title: How familiar were the depicted places to you?
elements.maxRateDescription: Very familiar / I know the places partly very well
elements.minRateDescription: Not familiar at all / I do not know these places

elements.name: familiarity_open
elements.title: If you were familiar with individual locations: To what extent did this familiarity influence your judgments of the images?

elements.name: criteria
elements.title: Please briefly describe the aspects that determined/influenced your decision to “keep” an image or give it a high rating.

elements.name: appreciation
elements.title: How much did you consider each of the following factors when judging image beauty?
elements.description: 1 = not at all … 7 = a lot. Factor labels are written out from the variable names in the open data (appreciation_*).

elements.name: beauty_importance
elements.title: How important is the beauty of the image when you think about whether you would keep an image in your ‘image collection’?
elements.description: 1 = not important at all … 7 = very important (anchor wording assumed; the open data give only the 1–7 range).

elements.name: object_importance
elements.title: In comparison: How important is the beauty of the scene or object depicted when you think about whether you would keep an image in your ‘image collection’?

elements.name: photofreq
elements.title: How often do you take photos yourself (whether with a smartphone or your own camera) of the various categories?
